characters: Madam Frimpomaa: the English teacher, in a yellow dress, with a stack of letters and a red pen.
Kwasi Cobbinah and Hannah: two Letter Club members, 14, with notebooks and pens.
Cousin Doreen: a girl of 14 in Cape Coast, far away, seen only in a photograph held by Kwasi.
The Letter Club room: a corner classroom with a chart of a letter with its parts labelled in coloured boxes.

narrationPlan.voice: Cheerful, clear teacher voice for Madam Frimpomaa; lively student voices
narrationPlan.pace: Bright and clear, slower at the parts of the letter (about 120 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: Light, cheerful marimba with a postal-bell chime; a satisfying finish (placeholder)
culturalNotes: The students, teacher and school are invented. The addresses are made up.
The story gives one widely taught pattern for an informal letter; teachers should check it against the current BECE syllabus and marking scheme and adapt it.
Closings such as “Yours ever”, “Your loving cousin” and “Your friend” are examples of warm, informal sign-offs.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?

Check every part of the letter format, including address position, date style, punctuation after the greeting and the sign-off, against the current BECE English marking scheme and the NaCCA English syllabus.
Check that the advice about contractions, abbreviations and chat words matches current WAEC guidance.
Check that the sample letter is warm, correct and suitable as a model.

teacherGuide.overview: A masterclass story that walks through the parts of an informal letter and shows exam-safe habits. It ends with a checklist learners can use for marking each other’s letters.
learningGoals: Name and order the parts of an informal letter.
Write a letter with details, linking words and a warm close.
Use a checklist to mark a letter fairly.
beforeReading: Ask: when did you last receive a handwritten letter or card? How did it feel?
whileReading: At each page, ask learners to point to the matching part on a chart.
afterReading: Write a full letter to a cousin using all six parts.
Swap letters and mark them with the checklist.
discussion: Why should a letter to a cousin still use full words?
What makes a letter feel warm?
reflection: Which part of the letter is easiest for you, and which is hardest?

support: Give learners a letter frame with labelled boxes and sentence starters.
stretch: Write the same news twice: once in chat voice, once in exam voice, and explain the differences.

culturalNotes: The students, teacher and school are invented. The addresses are made up.
The story gives one widely taught pattern for an informal letter; teachers should check it against the current BECE syllabus and marking scheme and adapt it.
Closings such as “Yours ever”, “Your loving cousin” and “Your friend” are examples of warm, informal sign-offs.
localiseThis: Use your learners’ real addresses, cousins and places. Check the format against your school’s English syllabus.

factCheck.claim: Informal letters include the sender’s address and date, a salutation (“Dear …”), an opening, a body in paragraphs, a conclusion and a friendly subscription such as “Yours ever” or “Your loving friend”.
factCheck.explanation: From a Ghana curriculum learning-material lesson on informal letters.
factCheck.reference: Ghana curriculum resources, “English Language LM Year 1 Section 15” (curriculumresources.edu.gh).

factCheck.claim: WAEC examiners have for years reported that candidates lose marks for text-style abbreviations and slang in letters; WAEC repeated the warning in September 2026.
factCheck.explanation: News reports of WAEC’s statement and of examiners’ concerns.
